sections.heading: Scalars, vectors and coordinates
bullets: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction. The zero vector has magnitude zero and no defined direction.
Vector addition is head-to-tail (or parallelogram) addition; subtraction is addition of the opposite vector. Scalar multiplication scales magnitude and reverses direction when the scalar is negative.
In R² or R³, perform addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication componentwise. The norm of a=(a₁,…,aₙ) is ||a||=√(a₁²+…+aₙ²); distance between points P and Q is ||Q−P||.
The standard basis vectors i,j,k have unit length and point along positive coordinate axes. A vector can be written as a₁i+a₂j+a₃k.

sections.heading: Dot product and projection
bullets: For vectors a,b, a·b=||a||||b||cos θ and in coordinates a·b=Σaᵢbᵢ. Thus cos θ=(a·b)/(||a||||b||). A zero dot product means orthogonality for nonzero vectors.
The scalar projection of a onto b is comp_b(a)=(a·b)/||b||; the vector projection is proj_b(a)=((a·b)/(b·b))b.
Direction cosines of a nonzero vector in R³ are its components divided by its norm; their squares sum to 1.
The dot product is useful for angles, perpendicularity, work and projections. It is commutative and distributes over vector addition.

sections.heading: Cross product and geometric applications
bullets: For a,b in R³, a×b is perpendicular to both, with magnitude ||a×b||=||a||||b||sin θ and direction given by the right-hand rule.
Compute the cross product using the determinant pattern with i,j,k, taking care of alternating signs. Parallel vectors have zero cross product.
Area of a parallelogram spanned by a,b is ||a×b||; area of the triangle is half of that.
The scalar triple product a·(b×c) gives signed parallelepiped volume; absolute value gives volume. A zero result means the vectors are coplanar/dependent.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Check whether a question asks for scalar or vector projection.
For cross products, verify perpendicularity by dotting the result with each original vector.
Use the sign of a scalar triple product for orientation and its absolute value for volume.

sections.heading: Lines and planes in three dimensions
bullets: A line through point r₀ with direction vector v is r=r₀+tv. In coordinates this gives parametric equations; if all direction components are nonzero, symmetric form uses (x−x₀)/v₁=(y−y₀)/v₂=(z−z₀)/v₃.
A plane through r₀ with normal n satisfies n·(r−r₀)=0, or ax+by+cz=d. The coefficients (a,b,c) form a normal vector.
Distance from point P(x₀,y₀,z₀) to plane ax+by+cz+d=0 is |ax₀+by₀+cz₀+d|/√(a²+b²+c²).
For line-plane relations, substitute the line parameter into the plane equation; a zero directional dot product indicates parallel direction, while a point satisfying both lies at intersection.

sections.heading: Vector spaces, subspaces and bases
bullets: A vector space is a set with vector addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the familiar algebraic laws (closure, associativity, identities, inverses and distributivity). Examples include Rⁿ and spaces of polynomials.

A subset W of a vector space is a subspace if it contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Equivalently, for any u,v in W and scalars c,d, cu+dv must remain in W.
A linear combination of vectors v₁,…,vₖ is c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ. Their span is the set of all such combinations.
Vectors are linearly independent when the only solution of c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ=0 is all cᵢ=0; otherwise they are dependent.
A basis is a linearly independent spanning set. Coordinates relative to a basis are unique, and the number of vectors in a finite basis is the dimension.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Translate between vector, parametric and symmetric line forms.
Identify a plane normal and use it to test parallelism or perpendicularity.
To test subspace, check zero and closure; to test independence, solve the associated homogeneous linear combination.

topics.title: Matrix operations, row reduction and inverse

sections.heading: Matrix basics and operations
bullets: A matrix is a rectangular array; its size is rows × columns. Addition is defined only for equal sizes and is componentwise.
Scalar multiplication multiplies every entry. Matrix multiplication AB is defined when columns of A equal rows of B; the result has rows of A and columns of B.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: AB need not equal BA. It is associative and distributes over addition when dimensions allow.
The identity matrix I satisfies AI=IA=A. The transpose Aᵀ exchanges rows and columns; for compatible matrices (AB)ᵀ=BᵀAᵀ.
The trace of a square matrix is the sum of diagonal entries. It is invariant under similarity and satisfies tr(A+B)=tr(A)+tr(B).

sections.heading: Elementary row operations and inverses
bullets: Elementary row operations are: interchange rows; multiply a row by a nonzero scalar; add a multiple of one row to another. They preserve the solution set of a linear system when applied to its augmented matrix.
Row echelon form has zero rows at the bottom and leading entries stepping right; reduced row echelon form also has leading 1s as the only nonzero entries in their columns.
A square matrix A is invertible if there exists A⁻¹ with AA⁻¹=A⁻¹A=I. Augment [A|I] and row reduce to [I|A⁻¹] when possible.
A is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero, its columns are independent, and Ax=0 has only the trivial solution.
(AB)⁻¹=B⁻¹A⁻¹; order reverses. Verify a proposed inverse by multiplication.

sections.heading: Determinants
bullets: For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det A=ad−bc. For larger matrices use cofactor expansion or row reduction, choosing a row/column with many zeros where possible.
Swapping two rows changes the determinant sign; multiplying a row by c multiplies determinant by c; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged.
For triangular matrices the determinant is the product of diagonal entries. det(AB)=det(A)det(B), and det(Aᵀ)=det(A).
A determinant measures signed volume scaling; det A=0 means the transformation collapses dimension and the matrix is singular.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Check dimensions before multiplying matrices and preserve the order of factors.
Use row operations carefully when computing determinants; record swaps and scalings.
When finding an inverse, verify that the matrix is square and nonsingular.

sections.heading: Solving linear systems
bullets: Write a system as Ax=b and form its augmented matrix [A|b]. Gaussian elimination reduces to echelon form; back-substitution then finds pivot variables.
A row [0 … 0 | c] with c≠0 signals inconsistency. Free variables indicate infinitely many solutions when the system is consistent; a pivot in every variable gives a unique solution.
Cramer’s rule for an n×n system with det A≠0 gives xᵢ=det(Aᵢ)/det(A), where Aᵢ replaces column i by b. It is mainly practical for small systems.
Inverse method x=A⁻¹b works only if A is square and invertible. Elimination is more general and usually more efficient.

sections.heading: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
bullets: A nonzero vector v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ if Av=λv. Solve (A−λI)v=0.
Eigenvalues satisfy the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0. For each λ, find a basis for the nullspace of A−λI to obtain eigenvectors.
Geometrically, an eigenvector direction is preserved by the linear transformation; λ gives its scaling and a negative λ reverses direction.
Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. Repeated eigenvalues may have fewer independent eigenvectors than their algebraic multiplicity.

sections.heading: Diagonalization
bullets: An n×n matrix is diagonalizable if it has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Form P from eigenvectors as columns and D from corresponding eigenvalues on the diagonal; then A=PDP⁻¹.
Keep eigenvector order consistent between P and D. Powers become Aᵏ=PDᵏP⁻¹, which can simplify repeated transformations.
A matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable; repeated eigenvalues require checking the dimension of each eigenspace.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Use row reduction to determine consistency and count free variables.
Check an eigenpair by direct substitution Av=λv.
Before diagonalizing, confirm there are enough independent eigenvectors and match their order in P and D.

sections.heading: Meaning and computation of limits
bullets: The limit limₓ→a f(x)=L describes values of f(x) approaching L as x approaches a, whether or not f(a) is defined or equals L.

For polynomials and rational functions, direct substitution works when the expression is defined at the target. If substitution gives 0/0, simplify, factor, rationalize or use an identity before taking the limit.
Limit laws allow sums, products, quotients (when limiting denominator is nonzero) and compositions to be handled from component limits.
A two-sided limit exists only when left-hand and right-hand limits both exist and are equal. A mismatch means the two-sided limit does not exist.

sections.heading: Infinite limits, asymptotes and continuity
bullets: An infinite limit describes unbounded behavior near a point and often indicates a vertical asymptote. Examine signs on either side; the directions can differ.
A limit at infinity studies end behavior. A finite limit as x→±∞ may give a horizontal asymptote; compare polynomial degrees or divide by the dominant power.
f is continuous at a if f(a) is defined, limₓ→a f(x) exists, and the limit equals f(a). Continuity on an interval requires continuity at every point there, with one-sided conditions at endpoints.
Removable discontinuity can be fixed by redefining a point; jump discontinuity has unequal one-sided limits; infinite discontinuity has unbounded behavior; oscillatory behavior may prevent a limit.
The Intermediate Value Theorem: if f is continuous on [a,b], every value between f(a) and f(b) is attained. In particular, opposite endpoint signs guarantee at least one root inside.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Classify indeterminate forms only after attempting algebraic simplification; 0/0 is not itself a limit answer.
Compare one-sided limits before asserting a two-sided limit.
For IVT, state continuity on a closed interval and show the target lies between endpoint values.

sections.heading: Derivative as rate and slope
bullets: The derivative f′(a)=limₕ→0 [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h, when the limit exists. It is the instantaneous rate of change and slope of the tangent line.
A function differentiable at a is continuous there, but continuity alone does not guarantee differentiability; corners, cusps, vertical tangents and discontinuities can prevent a finite derivative.
The tangent line at x=a is y−f(a)=f′(a)(x−a). Units of derivative are output units per input unit.

sections.heading: Core rules
bullets: Constant: d(c)/dx=0; power rule: d(xⁿ)/dx=nxⁿ⁻¹ where defined. Apply linearity: (cf+g)′=cf′+g′.
Product rule: (fg)′=f′g+fg′. Quotient rule: (f/g)′=(f′g−fg′)/g², g≠0.
Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x))=f′(g(x))g′(x). Identify the outer and inner functions explicitly for nested expressions.
Trigonometric derivatives: (sin x)′=cos x; (cos x)′=−sin x; (tan x)′=sec²x. The angle is in radians.
Exponential/log rules: (eˣ)′=eˣ; (aˣ)′=aˣ ln a; (ln x)′=1/x for x>0; (logₐx)′=1/(x ln a).

sections.heading: Implicit, higher and inverse derivatives
bullets: Implicit differentiation treats y as a function of x. Differentiate both sides with respect to x and use dy/dx whenever differentiating a term involving y.
Higher derivatives differentiate again: f″ describes change in slope and often acceleration when f is position; f⁽ⁿ⁾ denotes repeated differentiation.
For inverse functions, (f⁻¹)′(x)=1/f′(f⁻¹(x)) where the inverse exists and denominator is nonzero.
Inverse-trigonometric derivative patterns include (arcsin x)′=1/√(1−x²), (arctan x)′=1/(1+x²); respect domains and endpoint restrictions.
Logarithmic differentiation is useful for variable powers or products: take logarithms, differentiate implicitly, then solve for y′.
Hyperbolic functions are defined through exponentials; for example sinh x=(eˣ−e⁻ˣ)/2 and cosh x=(eˣ+e⁻ˣ)/2, with cosh²x−sinh²x=1. Their derivatives follow the corresponding hyperbolic identities.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Select the rule from the expression’s structure; nested functions require the chain rule.
Keep parentheses through product and quotient differentiation and simplify only after applying the rule.
When differentiating implicitly, include y′ for every y-dependent term.

sections.heading: Critical points and extrema
bullets: A critical number c is in the domain of f and has f′(c)=0 or f′(c) undefined. Local extrema can occur at critical numbers; absolute extrema on a closed interval can also occur at endpoints.
For absolute extrema on [a,b], evaluate f at all critical numbers inside and at both endpoints, then compare values.
Fermat’s theorem: if a differentiable function has a local extremum at an interior point, its derivative there is zero. The converse is not guaranteed.

sections.heading: First and second derivative tests
bullets: If f′ changes from positive to negative, f has a local maximum; negative to positive gives a local minimum. No sign change means no local extremum at that critical point.
f′>0 indicates increasing and f′<0 decreasing on an interval. Make a sign chart using critical numbers and domain breaks.
f″>0 indicates concave up; f″<0 concave down. A possible inflection point requires a change in concavity, not merely f″=0.
At a critical point c with f′(c)=0: f″(c)>0 gives a local minimum and f″(c)<0 a local maximum; if f″(c)=0, test is inconclusive.
Curve sketching combines domain, intercepts, symmetry, asymptotes, critical points, monotonicity, concavity and inflection points.

sections.heading: L’Hôpital’s rule, rates and optimization
bullets: L’Hôpital’s rule applies to limits in the indeterminate forms 0/0 or ∞/∞ when differentiability and denominator conditions are met: lim f/g=lim f′/g′ if the latter limit exists (or appropriate infinite limit). Do not use it on non-indeterminate quotients without first transforming them.

Related-rates problems connect quantities through an equation, differentiate with respect to time, then substitute the values at the specified instant. Include units and signs for increasing/decreasing quantities.

Optimization: define the objective, express it in one variable using constraints, determine the feasible domain, find critical points and endpoints, then justify which gives the required maximum or minimum.
A local test alone may not establish a global optimum; compare boundaries and check the real-world constraints.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Find and classify all critical points with a sign chart or derivative test.
Use L’Hôpital only after identifying a valid indeterminate form.
For optimization, state the objective function and feasible domain before differentiating.

sections.heading: Definite integral and properties
bullets: The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx is a limit of signed Riemann sums and represents net accumulated quantity; areas below the x-axis count negatively.
Linearity: ∫(cf+g)=c∫f+∫g. Reversing limits changes sign; splitting an interval is additive; ∫ₐᵃ f=0.
If f is continuous on [a,b], it is integrable. Comparison and symmetry can simplify calculations when conditions apply.
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects differentiation and integration: if F′=f, then ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx=F(b)−F(a). Also d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt=f(x) for continuous f.

sections.heading: Indefinite integrals and antiderivatives
bullets: An antiderivative F satisfies F′=f. The indefinite integral is ∫f(x)dx=F(x)+C; include the constant of integration.
Power rule for integration: ∫xⁿdx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C for n≠−1; ∫1/x dx=ln|x|+C.
Basic integrals reverse the derivative rules. Verify an antiderivative by differentiating it.
For definite integrals, evaluate an antiderivative at upper minus lower limits; do not add +C to the final numerical value.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish signed integral from geometric area; split at x-intercepts when finding total area.
Use FTC only after finding an antiderivative and substitute endpoints in the correct order.
Add +C to indefinite integrals and verify by differentiation.

sections.heading: Recognizing derivatives and substitution
bullets: Use substitution u=g(x) when the integrand contains a composite function and a factor proportional to g′(x). Then du=g′(x)dx and rewrite the entire integral in u.
For definite integrals, either convert both limits to u-values or substitute back before evaluating; do not mix variable and limits.
A sum is not integrated by a logarithm rule: log properties apply to products, quotients and powers, not arbitrary sums.

sections.heading: Integration by parts
bullets: Integration by parts follows the product rule: ∫u dv=uv−∫v du. Choose u to become simpler when differentiated and dv that is straightforward to integrate.
For repeated polynomial-times-exponential or trigonometric products, apply parts repeatedly or use a tabular approach while tracking signs.
For definite integrals, include boundary term [uv]ₐᵇ and evaluate the remaining definite integral.

sections.heading: Trigonometric substitution and integrals
bullets: For radicals involving √(a²−x²), use x=a sin θ; for √(a²+x²), use x=a tan θ; for √(x²−a²), use x=a sec θ, with domains and signs handled carefully.
Trigonometric integrals use identities such as sin²x=(1−cos2x)/2 and cos²x=(1+cos2x)/2. For powers, choose substitutions based on whether an odd power leaves a factor whose derivative is present.
After substitution, draw a reference triangle or use the substitution identity to return from θ to x and respect the original domain.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Choose substitution when a derivative pattern is present; choose parts for products where differentiation simplifies a factor.
Show the transformed differential and rewrite every occurrence of x before integrating.
Back-substitute and verify by differentiation whenever practical.

topics.title: Reduction formulas, partial fractions and other substitutions

sections.heading: Reduction formulas and partial fractions
bullets: A reduction formula expresses an integral with parameter n in terms of a simpler one (often n−1 or n−2). Establish the recurrence and base case before applying it repeatedly.
Partial fractions decompose a proper rational function into simpler fractions after factoring the denominator. If numerator degree is at least denominator degree, perform polynomial division first.
For distinct linear factors, use constants over each factor; for repeated factors include every power; for irreducible quadratic factors use a linear numerator over each relevant power.
Solve coefficients by clearing denominators and equating coefficients or substituting convenient roots, then integrate each term.

sections.heading: Tangent half-angle and irrational functions
bullets: The tangent half-angle substitution t=tan(x/2) gives sin x=2t/(1+t²), cos x=(1−t²)/(1+t²), and dx=2dt/(1+t²). It can convert rational expressions in sin and cos into rational functions of t.
For irrational integrals, select a substitution that simplifies the radical or transforms the expression into a rational form; state any domain restriction and back-substitute carefully.
Check for extraneous restrictions introduced by substitutions and ensure the transformed interval or branch corresponds to the original variable.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Make a rational function proper before partial fraction decomposition.
Write all terms for repeated and irreducible factors; omitting one changes the decomposition.
After substitution, express the final antiderivative in the original variable and check by differentiation.

sections.heading: Definition and convergence
bullets: An integral over an infinite interval is defined as a limit, for example ∫ₐ^∞f(x)dx=limᵦ→∞∫ₐᵇf(x)dx. It converges if the finite limit exists; otherwise it diverges.
If the integrand is unbounded at an endpoint or interior point, split the interval at the singularity and define each piece with a one-sided limit.
For ∫₁^∞x^(−p)dx, convergence occurs when p>1; near zero, ∫₀¹x^(−p)dx converges when p<1. Use comparison with these p-integrals where appropriate.
An improper integral with multiple infinite endpoints or singularities must be checked separately on every piece; convergence of the whole requires all pieces to converge.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Rewrite the improper integral as a limit before evaluating.
Locate all singularities and split the interval so each limit is one-sided and well-defined.
State whether the limit is finite; an antiderivative alone does not establish convergence.

sections.heading: Set up an area integral
bullets: Area between y=f(x) and y=g(x) on [a,b] is ∫ₐᵇ(top−bottom)dx, provided the same curve stays above throughout.
Find intersection points to determine bounds and split the interval wherever the upper and lower curves switch.
With horizontal slices, integrate right−left with respect to y. Choose the orientation that gives simpler bounds and fewer pieces.
Geometric area is nonnegative; if an integral represents signed area, use absolute value or split at crossings.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Sketch or analyze the curves to determine which is top/bottom or right/left.
Solve intersections before setting bounds.
Check that the integrand is nonnegative on each area interval.

sections.heading: Disk and washer methods
bullets: Cross-sectional area method: V=∫A(x)dx (or ∫A(y)dy) over the interval.
Disk method for rotation around an axis: V=π∫R². Washer method with a hole: V=π∫(R²−r²), where R is outer radius and r inner radius.
Radii are distances from the axis of rotation, not automatically the function value. For a shifted axis, subtract the axis coordinate.
Use slices perpendicular to the axis of rotation for disks/washers; express radii in the same variable as the integration bounds.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Sketch the region and axis, then draw a representative slice.
Identify outer and inner radii before squaring; do not subtract radii after squaring incorrectly.
Check units: integrating area over length gives cubic units.

topics.title: Cylindrical shells and choosing a method

sections.heading: Shell method
bullets: For cylindrical shells, volume is V=2π∫(radius)(height)(thickness). With vertical shells, integrate in x; with horizontal shells, integrate in y.
Radius is distance from the shell to the axis; height is the length of the region along the shell. If the region or axis shifts, compute these distances explicitly.
Shells are useful when slices parallel to the axis avoid splitting the region or solving for the inverse function, while disks/washers use slices perpendicular to the axis.
The method is a Riemann-sum limit of thin cylindrical layers; the factor 2πr is circumference and height×thickness gives the rectangular side area.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Decide between shell and washer methods by the orientation of slices relative to the rotation axis.
Label radius, height and thickness on a sketch before forming the integral.
Compare the shell setup with a disk/washer setup when the first expression is difficult.

topics.title: Arc length of explicit and parametric curves

sections.heading: Arc-length formulas
bullets: For y=f(x) on [a,b], arc length L=∫ₐᵇ√(1+[f′(x)]²)dx, assuming a sufficiently smooth curve.
For a parametric curve x=x(t), y=y(t), t∈[α,β], L=∫αᵝ√[(dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²]dt.
Arc length comes from summing small straight-line segments and taking a limit; the square root combines horizontal and vertical changes by the Pythagorean theorem.
If the curve is easier as x=g(y), use L=∫√(1+[dx/dy]²)dy.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Differentiate the curve before substituting into the arc-length formula.
Use parameter bounds corresponding to the exact curve segment requested.
Simplify the radical and check whether an exact antiderivative is available; numerical evaluation may be needed otherwise.

sections.heading: Surface-area formulas
bullets: Rotating y=f(x) about the x-axis gives surface area S=2π∫ₐᵇ |y|√(1+[y′]²)dx when the curve does not cross the axis; the radius is distance to the axis.
For rotation about the y-axis using x as parameter, S=2π∫ₐᵇ |x|√(1+[y′]²)dx. If integrating with respect to y, rewrite the curve and use the corresponding arc-length element.
The general idea is circumference 2πr multiplied by a small arc-length segment ds. The differential ds is √(1+(dy/dx)²)dx or its parametric equivalent.
If the curve crosses the axis or the radius changes sign relative to the axis, split the interval or use absolute distance so the surface area remains nonnegative.

sections.heading: Final exam review
bullets: Distinguish volume integrals from surface-area integrals: volume uses cross-sectional area or shells; surface area uses circumference times arc length.
Identify the axis and compute radius as distance to it, not simply y or x unless the axis is a coordinate axis and the curve lies on one side.
Check the differential length factor and ensure the final units are square units.
